questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: A native English speaking country and not to far away from home.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I got most of the information needed before or just after I arrived through email. It was easy to understand and follow.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Two introduction days the week before classes started at UCC which answered the most pressing questions about the academic aspect. Furthermore a group for international students in Cork was available. They arranged meetups and trips during the whole semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of options, more limited if you are only staying for one semester. The UCC has a good webpage with the different housing options and a service that can help you. If you start looking in good time there are a lot of options but I was a little late out and could only find one place with free rooms. So start 3-4 months in advance before your offical acceptance from the univeristy (for me UCC) and put down the deposit. There is a quite good chance to get accepted to UCC if you have been forwarded by your university.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In general the housing is very expensive not matter where you live. There are some that a quite far from campus and the public transportation system is very unreliable so either you need to leave early or be late. I got a bike which worked really well for me but it was not for everyone since they drive on the opposite side compared to many countries. If I had had the option to choose something closer to campus I would. Also it is a good idea to inquire about if there is a duvet and pillow as well as kitchen utentiels (plates, cutlery, pans, pots etc.) because some places don't provide those. For example, if you arrive late and the shops are closed you will need to spend the first night without a duvet.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UCC has swap shop where former students has left a abundance of things. Go there before buyng everything new

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Before you arrive (1-2 weeks) you get a link through email and you need to choose your modules. For many of them the timetable is not available yet so you choose blindly. Then when you arrive you start getting accepted or rejected from modules based on timetable conflict, full classes etc. It is then possible to change modules if you get rejected and now most timetables are available. This process is first done 2-3 weeks into the start of the semester when classes has begun.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could write to the international office and get some guidance.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got rejected to 3 classes, mostly due to timetable conflict, and ended  up choosing some outside my department because non of the other fit

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: to be patience and not panic or stress to much when you get rejected and how long it takes before everything is approved. And have a lot of modules to choose from because most get rejected from at least one.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If your modules are from at a lot of different departments and covering a lot of years there is a risk of overlapping exams. If that happens you take them just after each other in a special room with an hour break between.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was in my last year of my BA (biochemistry) and took 3rd and 4th year modules within my subject and some 1st year modules in history

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
At UCC there are mostly lectures where there at UCPH also is theoretical excises. Also the syllabus is not firm at UCC. You can choose your own book(s) and you need to find the right chapters and pages that fits the lecture on your own. It is more optional to read and everything is covered in the lectures. What is really nice is that most books are avaliable for free at the library or as e-boks through the library. On the other hand, at UCPH, specific pages and chapters are connected to each lecture and they are more overview style.
In connection to assessment at UCC most modules have some part of continues assesement and some don't have a closing exam but only continues assesement. Also most exams are written and only 1.5 hour long.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
HI1115: Modern Irish History for international students.
BC3004: cell signalling.
MB3022: virology. 
PT3001: introduction to pharmacology.
PT4005: neuropharmacology
CC1110: Celts: the origins.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The two pharmacology classes were really interesting and I learned a lot but also hard. There was so much stuff to learn, far above what is normally included in a 5 ECTS module. I would recommend taking both of them if you haven't taken any prior pharmacology classes since neuropharmacology builds on top of introduction to pharmacology.
Also CC1110 was really fun and I enjoyed learning something completely outside my expertise. The exam was also low effort which was nice to have because some of the others required a lot of work.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went out a lot more than usual. Both for dinner with friends, to pubs, clubs and on trips around Ireland

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It was in general less expensive to buy groceries but most things (e.g., eating out) was the same as in Denmark. The rent was very expensive compared to DK but I was warned beforehand so it wasn't unexpected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There is a lot of sport clubs (climbing, Gaelic football etc.) and societies (academic, Harry Potter etc.) available. Most of them have beginner classes at the beginning of the semester. Also a big sports centre where there is classes (e.g., spinning, yoga etc.) for free or train in the gym. 
There is also a big group (watchapp) for international students in Cork across the different univeristies that arrange trips and other events.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The mountaineering club plan beginner hiking trips to beautiful locations that are difficult to get to without a car.  
If you want to try a new activity (sport) it is a good place to do it because it's free to try and there are a lot of beginners classes. But if you are already good at something there are also advanced teams. It is also a good way to meet new people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is not really any holidays but it is nice to do trips to different cities in the weekends. Kinsale and Cobh are nice coast cities. Also a trip to Galway or around Kerry. You can do it yourself if you rent a car or the international group plans weekend trips. There is also a lot of events/places in and near the city: iceskating, escape room, cinema, Blarney Castle etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture is in most ways very similar to Denmark. What was most different was the going out culture. The Irish students went out during the week and home in the weekends. Also the pubs and clubs closed kind of early (at the latest 2 am) every day. Also everything that is not academic is late: when it says the party starts at 10 it will probably first begin at 11.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open and friendly. The Irish people are very nice but if you take classes above 1st year they already know each other and has formed groups so it's difficult to get to know them properly. If you have labs that's a good way to get started or via clubs and sociaties

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The public transportation was late and very unreliable. Minimum 10-15 min late and at the most I experienced 40 min (during the day). Also how everything is late. For example with module acceptance and exam dates (end of november).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The going out culture was really nice. There was always a place with live music and a lot of different pubs, bars and clubs with different atmospheres after your mood.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy it and try to get outside you comfort zone. It is going to fly by so fast.
2. Go to as many events and trips as you want. Remember it is okay to take a break from everything once in a while. It isn't dangerouse to miss out on one or two things.
3. It is worth it even though there is a lot of work before and after.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people and making friends from all over the world and getting to know them and learning about their counties and cultures.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To remember to study. It all kind of accumulated at the end so the last weeks were filled with a lot of studying and stress.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
